title: Capacity resilience playbook - iter 7 (NW + edge mirror pools)
body:
Summary

This is iteration 7 of the capacity resilience playbook focused on stabilizing the northwest region and validating the edge mirror pool concept. Goal is to reduce customer-impacting outages from regional GPU pressure, provide fast fallback options, and tighten the detection-to-remediation loop. Iteration 7 is intentionally pragmatic: prefer safe, observable changes we can revert quickly.

Key outcomes we want this week
- Prototype an automated mirror-pool failover for 2 small customers (non-critical test tenants) in NW region by Fri 2026-07-24
- Update capacity model with short-window surge factors and publish new run-rate table to the sheet linked above
- Run a chaos-lite exercise: simulate a 30% GPU preemption in nw-1 for 15 minutes and validate routing/fallback behavior
- Create 3 concise runbook pages for oncall: mirror-pool rollback, graceful degrade to quantized model, and regional routing override

Background and rationale
- Recent spikes in conversational workload plus a sudden consumer app launch caused sustained high queue depth in nw-1. We saw longer tail latencies and 2 customer incidents last month.
- Our previous mitigations (aggressive prewarming and autoscale policies) reduced impact but require manual triage and are expensive. Mirror pools aim to provide an intermediate-cost, quick fallback without heavy autoscale churn.

What is a mirror pool (short)
- A small set of preinitialized nodes in a nearby region or on different instance types that host compatible model variants (same weights but different quantization or shorter sequence length tuning). They are kept warm and used as a routing target when primary pools approach latency SLO breach thresholds.
- Mirror pools are not full capacity replacements, but reduce error budget drain and buy time for autoscale or ticketed capacity fixes.

Prototype plan (NW region)
- Owner: Marco Li
- Scope: 2 test tenants (tenant-alpha, tenant-beta) routed through a canary policy to mirror-pool in west-1 when 95th percentile latency for primary pool > 1200ms for 1 minute
- Steps:
  - Create mirror pool nodes with light-weight quantized variants (Q8) and set KV cache TTL to 30s
  - Implement routing policy flag in smart-router: mirror_flag = true for test tenants
  - Add metric alerts: mirror-failover-triggered, mirror-latency, mirror-error-rate
  - Run load test 1: baseline latency profile, then spike 2x tokens/s and observe failover behavior
- Success criteria:
  - Failover happens automatically within 30s of threshold and reduces 95th latency by >= 30% for affected requests
  - No unhandled 500 errors attributed to model incompatibility

Capacity model updates required
- Owner: Carmen Ruiz
- Action: add short-window surge factor columns for 5-min, 15-min, and 60-min windows; include mirror-pool headroom as a separate line item
- Deliverable: new tab in the spreadsheet with 'surge-adjusted reserve' and a one-paragraph explanation of assumptions

Chaos-lite exercise (SRE + runtime)
- Owner: Owen McBride
- Window: Tuesday 2026-07-21 02:00-03:30 UTC
- Simulation: mark 30% of GPUs in nw-1 as preempted; routing layer should detect resource pressure and route eligible traffic to mirror-pool or west-1
- Observability checklist:
  - Traces sampled at 100% for failing requests during window
  - Synthetic canary queries for both test tenants every 15s
  - Confirm alert noise does not exceed 3 actionable alerts per 30 minutes

Open risks and unknowns
- Model compatibility: quantized variants could produce regressions for some prompts. Need small eval set for tenant-alpha and tenant-beta before promotion.
- Cold-starts for mirror pools may still be costly if KV cache contents are large; measurement needed.
- Billing/Cost: mirror pools increase steady-state cost; finance wants an estimate of incremental monthly cost for a 5-10 node mirror pool per region.

Decision log (this iteration)
- Use Q8 quantized variants for mirror-pool prototypes (decision made 2026-07-20, owner: Samira Khan)
- Limit mirror usage to tenants that opt-in for trial to reduce blast radius

Action items (short checklist)
- [ ] Marco: spin up mirror instances and push image with Q8 variant (due 2026-07-22)
- [ ] Carmen: publish updated capacity sheet and short assumptions blurb (due 2026-07-22)
- [ ] Owen: schedule chaos-lite window and update oncall runbook (due 2026-07-21)
- [ ] Samira: create small eval harness for tenant prompts and run A/B comfort check (due 2026-07-23)
- [ ] Aisha: sync with finance for cost estimate and include in runbook (due 2026-07-23)

Notes to self / loose ends
- If mirror-pool fails more than 2 times during prototype, pause and debug before expanding. Possible root causes: routing mismatch, unexpected weight/hash differences, or sequence-len mismatch.
- Check INFRA-2345 for previous mirror experiments and lessons learned, especially node boot times and docker runtime configs.
- Follow up with product to see if tenant list for trial can be expanded to include an internal sandbox team.

Meeting cadence and communication
- Weekly sync: Tue 09:30 PT short triage and status updates (owners only)
- Post-mortem call if chaos-lite causes any customer-visible impact; otherwise 1 pager summary to infra-all and product-ops
- Update the console dashboard with mirror usage metric by 2026-07-25 (owner: observability team)

Appendix: quick references
- Routing flag PR: github link in linked artifacts
- Capacity model spreadsheet: link above
- Related Jira: INFRA-2345 (mirror pool workstream), INFRA-2391 (capacity modelling fixes)

Questions for the group
- Would product be comfortable making mirror routing opt-in per tenant, or require org-level opt-in? Tradeoffs: finer control vs operational complexity.
- Is there appetite to try heterogeneous instance types for mirror pools (ie. different GPU class) rather than same type across regions? This could reduce cost but increase variance in latency profiles.

End of draft. Intend to iterate after prototype results.
